text: Every lesson so far has pulled data out of AdventureWorks2012. Real pipelines also push data in -- logging a run, writing cleaned results to a staging table, loading a transformed dataset. This lesson covers the mechanics of writing back.

Here's a single INSERT with execute. Notice the question mark -- that's a placeholder. The actual value, Test Category, is passed as a separate argument, never pasted directly into the SQL string. Lesson 29 explains exactly why that matters.

When you've got a whole list of rows to insert, executemany runs the same parameterized statement once per row. It's far faster than calling execute in a Python for loop, because the driver can batch the round trips to the server.

Here's the detail that trips people up: pyodbc connections are not in autocommit mode by default. Every insert, update, or delete sits inside an open transaction until you call conn.commit. Forget that line, and closing the connection silently discards the work.

Data engineers rarely write straight into a production table. More often, a pipeline truncates a staging table first, then loads into it -- so a bad load can be inspected or re-run without touching a table other systems depend on.

That question-mark placeholder you just saw isn't optional styling -- it's a security boundary. Next lesson digs into exactly what goes wrong without it: SQL injection, and how parameterized queries prevent it.
